name: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC)

summary.text: The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries was founded at a conference in Baghdad in September 1960 by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela. Its Persian Gulf members raised posted prices in October 1973, during the Arab embargo of the United States, and at the Tehran meeting of December 23, 1973 set a posted price of $11.60 for Gulf crude, more than double the previous level. Prices were broadly stable in nominal terms through 1978 and roughly doubled again in 1979-80 after the Iranian revolution. The U.S. record of these decisions is in the FRUS Energy Crisis volumes and contemporary CIA and GAO reports.

facts.claim: OPEC was founded in Baghdad in September 1960 by five countries. OPEC's own 2018 anniversary release names the founders as Juan Pablo Perez Alfonzo (Venezuela), Abdullah al-Tariki (Saudi Arabia), Tala'at al-Shaibani (Iraq), Fuad Rouhani (Iran) and Ahmed Sayed Omar (Kuwait).
facts.quote: Juan Pablo Perez Alfonzo (Venezuela), Abdullah al-Tariki (Saudi Arabia), Dr Tala'at al-Shaibani (Iraq), Dr Fuad Rouhani (Iran), and Ahmed Sayed Omar (Kuwait)

facts.claim: The State Department's Office of the Historian records that the 1973 embargo was imposed by Arab members of OPEC against the United States in retaliation for the U.S. resupply of Israel, banning petroleum exports to the targeted countries and introducing production cuts. A CIA memorandum of October 19, 1973 reported Saudi Arabia had cut production by about 10 percent and that several Arab producers had announced or threatened a total embargo against the United States.
facts.quote: several countries, including Libya, Abu Dhabi, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia, have either announced or threatened a total embargo against the United States

facts.claim: At the OPEC meeting in Tehran on December 23, 1973, Iranian Finance Minister Amouzegar announced a new posted price of $11.60 for Persian Gulf crude, an increase of more than 100 percent, effective January 1, 1974. A CIA report of January 4, 1974 described the figure as a compromise between the $5.50 per barrel increase favoured by the Shah and the $1.25 rise reportedly suggested by Saudi Oil Minister Yamani.
facts.quote: at the conclusion of the OPEC meeting in Tehran on December 23, Amouzegar announced a new posted price of $11.60 for Persian Gulf crude, an increase of more than 100 percent

facts.claim: In August 1974 the U.S. embassy in Jidda reported that Saudi Arabia's Cabinet had agreed to hold the line against any price increase at the September 1974 OPEC meeting, where Iran demanded a 35 percent rise and a compromise of $2.00 to $2.50 a barrel was discussed. In November 1974 the Shah told Kissinger he would propose at the December 12 OPEC meeting a single price system about $1.65 below the existing $11.65 level and a freeze for the first nine months of 1975.
facts.quote: The Cabinet had agreed that at the OPEC meeting the end of September Saudi Arabia must hold the line against any price increase.

facts.claim: In September 1975 President Ford wrote to the Shah before the OPEC price decision, arguing that another increase would hurt the U.S., European, Japanese and developing economies; the Shah replied with reasons an increase would be justified.
facts.quote: The letter argues that another increase would hurt the U.S., European, Japanese, and developing economies.

facts.claim: The Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago's 1994 account states that after the 1973-74 shock OPEC again asserted its influence in 1979 by cutting production and raising prices, when the loss of Iranian output and precautionary buying let prices rise faster than Saudi Arabia intended.
facts.quote: faced with the prospect of losing some control over the market, OPEC again asserted its influence in 1979 by cutting production and raising prices

connections.claim: Iran was a founding member of OPEC (1960) and hosted the December 23, 1973 Tehran meeting at which the Persian Gulf posted price was set at $11.60, a decision U.S. and Saudi documents attribute chiefly to the Shah.
connections.quote: Saudi officials had been against them and Shah chiefly to blame

openQuestions: The October 16, 1973 Kuwait decision by the Gulf OPEC members to raise posted prices by about 70 percent to $5.11-5.12 is recorded only in secondary accounts here (CSIS, OGJ) and in a passing reference in FRUS vol. XXXVI Doc. 271 ($5.12); the FRUS document on the October 16 decision was not surfaced. The 1979-80 OPEC decisions are sourced to a Chicago Fed letter and a Statistics Norway price table rather than to FRUS vol. XXXVII, which was not searched document by document.

A CRS report giving the posted-price history was not found; the closest CRS product returned was RL31608 (The Effects of Oil Shocks on the Economy), which covers economic effects rather than the price series.
